s2.title: A sentence cut into tokens

s3.chapterTitle: Your question is chopped into tokens
s3.title: The context window fills up
s3.caption: Your question, the chat so far and the answer being written all share one fixed space. When it's full, something has to give: many apps drop or summarise the oldest messages.

s4.chapterTitle: Each word becomes a point in space
s4.title: Token numbers versus embeddings
s4.caption: A token number is just a label. An embedding is a pattern of numbers, and similar meanings get similar patterns. Values made up for this example.
s4.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 368" role="img" aria-labelledby="s4-illEmT s4-illEmD" width="100%">
    <title id="s4-illEmT">Token numbers versus embeddings</title>
    <desc id="s4-illEmD">Top: token numbers 9,412, 9,413 and 9,414 stand for sky, jumped and Paris. Next-door numbers, unrelated words. Bottom: each word's embedding is drawn as a strip of coloured cells. The strips for sky and cloud have almost the same pattern. The strip for sandwich looks quite different. Similar patterns mean similar meanings.</desc>
    <g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif" fill="#231F20" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32)">
      <text x="20" y="28" font-size="13" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".08em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:13px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:1.04px">TOKEN NUMBERS</text>
      <rect x="20" y="44" width="72" height="26" fill="#ece8de" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1" style="fill:rgb(236, 232, 222);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32)"></rect><text x="56" y="62" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;text-anchor:middle">9,412</text><text x="102" y="62" font-size="15" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px">→ “sky”</text><rect x="20" y="76" width="72" height="26" fill="#ece8de" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1" style="fill:rgb(236, 232, 222);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32)"></rect><text x="56" y="94" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;text-anchor:middle">9,413</text><text x="102" y="94" font-size="15" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px">→ “jumped”</text><rect x="20" y="108" width="72" height="26" fill="#ece8de" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1" style="fill:rgb(236, 232, 222);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32)"></rect><text x="56" y="126" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;text-anchor:middle">9,414</text><text x="102" y="126" font-size="15" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px">→ “Paris”</text>

s7.chapterTitle: The trip to a building full of chips
s7.title: Your question's journey to a data centre
s7.caption: Cloud AI: the model runs in a data centre, and you reach it over the internet. Running the already-trained model to answer you is inference.
s7.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 236" role="img" aria-labelledby="s7-illCdT s7-illCdD" width="100%">
    <title id="s7-illCdT">Your question's journey to a data centre</title>
    <desc id="s7-illCdD">Your phone sends the question as pulses of light along a fibre-optic cable, which may run under the sea, to a data centre full of racks of chips. Inference happens there: the trained model runs. The answer streams back along the same route, token by token.</desc>
    <g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif" fill="#231F20" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32)">
      <text x="220" y="24" font-size="15" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;font-weight:700;text-anchor:middle">Question →  travels as light</text>

s8.chapterTitle: Thousands of workers, one huge sum
s8.title: Multiplying a matrix: many separate sums
s8.caption: A matrix multiplication is lots of small, separate sums, which is exactly the kind of work thousands of GPU cores can share. Real models use grids with thousands of rows and columns.
s8.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 252" role="img" aria-labelledby="s8-illMxT s8-illMxD" width="100%">
    <title id="s8-illMxT">Multiplying a matrix: many separate sums</title>
    <desc id="s8-illMxD">A four-by-four grid of the model's numbers is multiplied by a column of four numbers for one token. Each of the four results is its own sum of one row times the column, for example 2 times 1 plus 0 times 2 plus 1 times 0 plus 3 times 1 equals 5. No sum waits for another, so all four can be worked out at the same time.</desc>

s9.chapterTitle: Thousands of workers, one huge sum
s9.title: Quantisation: fewer bits, rounded numbers
s9.caption: 4 bits allow only 16 different values, so every number is rounded to the nearest one: a quarter of the memory, a little less precision. Simplified: real methods also store a scale for each group of numbers.

s10.chapterTitle: Printing with light no one can see
s10.title: Who builds an AI chip
s10.caption: Simplified: hundreds more companies supply tools, chemicals and parts. Each one builds on the others, so a problem with any single link, such as an export ban, can hold up the whole chain.
s10.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 724" role="img" aria-labelledby="s10-illScT s10-illScD" width="100%">
    <title id="s10-illScT">Who builds an AI chip</title>
    <desc id="s10-illScD">The supply chain for one AI chip. Design: NVIDIA in the USA designs it, using chip-design software from Synopsys and Cadence. Machines: ASML in the Netherlands builds the EUV machines, using mirrors from Zeiss and lasers from Trumpf in Germany. Materials: silicon wafers from Shin-Etsu and SUMCO in Japan, and gallium and germanium mostly from China. All three flow into making: TSMC in Taiwan prints the design onto wafers. Memory chips called HBM come from SK hynix and Samsung in South Korea and Micron in the USA. TSMC packages the chip and its memory together, giving an AI chip ready for a data centre. At least seven countries are involved, and none can do it alone.</desc>

s11.chapterTitle: The model guesses the next word, again and again
s11.title: Attention: "blue" looks back at the words before it
s11.caption: Each token gives every earlier token a score, then blends in information from the ones that score highest. It can't look ahead: the words after it haven't been written yet.
s11.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 330" role="img" aria-labelledby="s11-illAtT s11-illAtD" width="100%">
    <title id="s11-illAtT">Attention: "blue" looks back at the words before it</title>
    <desc id="s11-illAtD">The tokens Why, is, the, sky, blue and a question mark. Curved lines run from "blue" back to each earlier token. The line to "sky" is by far the thickest: blue gives sky 75 percent of its attention, the others 5 or 10 percent. The question mark comes later, so blue cannot look at it. After attention, "blue" no longer means a colour or a mood: it means the colour of the sky.</desc>

s12.chapterTitle: The model guesses the next word, again and again

s13.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s13.title: Training: guess, check, nudge, repeat
s13.caption: Training adjusts the parameters a tiny bit after every guess. After training they're fixed: answering your question (inference) changes nothing. Percentages made up for this example.
s13.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s13-illTrT s13-illTrD" width="100%">
    <title id="s13-illTrT" style="font-size:18.02px">Training: guess, check, nudge, repeat</title>
    <desc id="s13-illTrD" style="font-size:18.02px">The model reads "The sky is" from its training text, with the next word hidden. It guesses: blue 30 percent, green 25 percent, grey 15 percent. It checks the real next word, which is blue. Then its parameters are nudged so that blue scores a little higher next time, 30 percent becomes 33 percent. This repeats for every token, trillions of times, over months.</desc>

s14.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s14.title: One model, many sources: DeepSeek-V3
s14.caption: DeepSeek-V3 mixes ideas from US and Chinese labs, and its own ideas were then picked up in both countries. Simplified: only some of its parts are shown. Source: Sebastian Raschka, "How LLMs build on each other" (llm-gallery.com).

s15.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s15.title: Closed models and open-weight models
s15.caption: Open weights let anyone build on a model, which is how ideas spread between labs, including across borders. Most come with a licence that sets some rules.
s15.svg:

s16.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s16.title: Distillation: a small student learns from a big teacher

s17.chapterTitle: The answer comes home, and you check it
s17.title: A hallucination looks just as sure as a fact
s17.caption: Fluent and confident isn't the same as correct. The only way to catch it was to check against a trusted source. (Blue taken as 450 nm, red as 700 nm.)
s17.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 330" role="img" aria-labelledby="s17-illHaT s17-illHaD" width="100%">
    <title id="s17-illHaT">A hallucination looks just as sure as a fact</title>
    <desc id="s17-illHaD">Two sentences from the chatbot's answer, written in exactly the same confident style. The first, shorter wavelengths scatter far more than longer ones, is right. The second, the effect depends on the wavelength to the power of two, is wrong. Your notes say intensity goes as one over wavelength to the power four, which shows the second sentence is a hallucination. It matters: with the right formula, blue light at 450 nanometres scatters about 6 times more than red at 700 nanometres. The wrong formula gives only about 2.4 times.</desc>
    <g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif" fill="#231F20" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32)">
      <text x="20" y="24" font-size="13" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".08em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:13px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:1.04px">THE ANSWER ON YOUR SCREEN</text>
      <rect x="20" y="36" width="400" height="40" fill="#fff" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5" style="fill:rgb(255, 255, 255);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32);stroke-width:1.5px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="61" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">Shorter wavelengths scatter far more than longer ones.</text>
      <rect x="20" y="84" width="400" height="40" fill="#fde8e8" stroke="#d93025" stroke-width="2.5" style="fill:rgb(253, 232, 232);stroke:rgb(217, 48, 37);stroke-width:2.5px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="109" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">It depends on the wavelength to the power of two.</text>
      <rect x="20" y="140" width="190" height="62" fill="#FFF3C4" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5" style="fill:rgb(255, 243, 196);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32);stroke-width:1.5px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="160" font-size="12" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".06em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:12px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:0.72px">YOUR NOTES</text>
      <text x="32" y="188" font-family="Georgia,'Times New Roman',serif" font-size="18" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:18px">I ∝ 1/λ⁴</text>
      <path d="M216 171H262V134" fill="none" stroke="#d93025" stroke-width="2" style="fill:none;stroke:rgb(217, 48, 37);stroke-width:2px"></path><path d="M262 128l-5 10h10z" fill="#d93025" style="fill:rgb(217, 48, 37)"></path>
      <text x="274" y="160" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#9b1c14" style="fill:rgb(155, 28, 20);font-size:14px;font-weight:700">Checked: the</text>
      <text x="274" y="178" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#9b1c14" style="fill:rgb(155, 28, 20);font-size:14px;font-weight:700">second sentence</text>
      <text x="274" y="196" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#9b1c14" style="fill:rgb(155, 28, 20);font-size:14px;font-weight:700">is a hallucination</text>
      <text x="220" y="228" font-size="14" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px;font-weight:700;text-anchor:middle">Both sounded equally sure. Only one was right.</text>
      <rect x="20" y="242" width="400" height="76" fill="#fff" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.2" style="fill:rgb(255, 255, 255);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32);stroke-width:1.2px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="264" font-size="13" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".06em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:13px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:0.78px">WHY IT MATTERS</text>
      <text x="32" y="286" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">Blue vs red light: with λ⁴, blue scatters about 6× more.</text>
      <text x="32" y="306" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">With the wrong λ², it would be only about 2.4×.</text>
    </g>
  </svg>

s18.chapterTitle: The answer comes home, and you check it
s18.title: Cloud AI and edge AI
s18.caption: Green marks each one's advantage. Dots stand for parameters, not to scale: big cloud models have hundreds of billions, small ones a few billion. Quantisation and distillation (chapters 4 and 8) help big models fit on devices too.

s31.title: One assistant, three pieces

s32.title: Three workflow shapes
s32.caption: In all three, people fix the steps in advance. The AI does the work inside each step.

s33.chapterTitle: Check it, vote on it, try again
s33.title: What each check has to go on
s33.caption: A check is only as good as what it checks against. Reflection has the least to go on; a vote needs some randomness (temperature) so the answers can differ.
s33.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 302" role="img" aria-labelledby="s33-ill2T s33-ill2D" width="100%">
    <title id="s33-ill2T">What each check has to go on</title>
    <desc id="s33-ill2D">Three ways a model's answer gets checked, and what each is compared with. Reflection: the model rereads its own draft with its own judgement, with nothing from outside, so it can miss its own blind spots. Evaluator: the draft is checked against a mark scheme of stated criteria, so it is only as good as its criteria. Vote: the answer is compared with other answers to the same question, such as 5p, 5p, 10p, 5p, 5p, so it only works if the answers vary.</desc>

s37.title: How bias gets in, and how it can grow
s37.caption: Bias usually starts in the data: a model copies the patterns in past decisions, including unfair ones. If its own decisions are fed back in as new data, the gap can grow. Made-up numbers.

s38.title: Fair by which measure?
s38.caption: Fairness has more than one definition, and they can't always all be met at once. A tool can look equally accurate for two groups while its mistakes land much harder on one of them, so each group is checked on the measure that matters for the decision. Made-up numbers.

s40.title: What being open about AI covers
s40.caption: Transparency means telling people that AI is being used, what it was built from, where it fails and who is responsible. A model card is one common way to write this down. In the EU, the AI Act has required telling people and labelling AI-generated content since August 2026.

s44.title: Hitting the target, missing the point
s44.caption: AI is trained on something measurable that stands in for what we really want. When the two drift apart, the model can hit the target and miss the point: researchers call this specification gaming. Flattering people, sycophancy, is one result that has been linked to training on human ratings.

s45.title: The red-team loop
s45.caption: Red teams try to break a model before the public does. Every failure they find becomes a fix, and a new test so it stays fixed. Red teaming finds problems; it can't prove a model is safe.

s46.title: How a text watermark can work
s46.caption: One research method (Kirchenbauer and others, 2023): before each word, a secret key splits the possible next words into green and red halves, and the model is nudged towards green. s49.title: Same AI, different rules, depending on use
s49.caption: The EU AI Act sets rules by use, not by technology. Its bans have applied since February 2025 and its transparency rules since August 2026; dates for high-risk rules have been under review. The UK has no single AI law and relies mainly on existing laws, such as data protection and equality law.

s50.title: Two copyright questions
s50.caption: In the UK, text and data mining of others' work is clearly allowed only for non-commercial research (section 29A of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988); in 2026 the government dropped a proposed broad exception for AI training. Ownership of AI-made work is still being settled.

Going in: can a company train on people's work? In UK law, mining others' work is clearly allowed only for non-commercial research, so commercial training generally needs permission or a licence. Coming out: who owns what the AI makes, and does it copy anyone? s51.title: Three questions for an "AI-powered" claim
s51.caption: AI washing is overclaiming AI to ride the hype. Regulators have acted: in March 2024 the US Securities and Exchange Commission fined two investment firms for AI claims they could not back up.
s51.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s51-t s51-d"><title id="s51-t">Three questions for an "AI-powered" claim</title><desc id="s51-d">To test a product's AI claim, ask: what exactly does the AI do, could it be done without AI, and where is the evidence? s52.title: Approved tool or shadow AI?
s52.caption: Shadow AI is using AI tools that haven't been approved. The risk is less the tool itself than what happens to the data, and that nobody responsible knows it's being used.

Through an approved school tool, a data agreement controls how it is stored, it is not used for training, and the school can help if something goes wrong. s56.caption: Activation steering finds a direction inside the model by comparing contrasting prompts, then adds it while the model answers. It changes this reply, not the model itself, and too much can make replies strange.

s60.title: How an uncensored model differs from a jailbreak
s60.caption: An uncensored model has its refusals removed from the file itself, unlike a jailbreak, which tricks an unchanged model. Because it runs on someone's own computer, nobody can patch it. Illegal content is still illegal, whichever tool makes it.
s60.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s60-t s60-d"><title id="s60-t">How an uncensored model differs from a jailbreak</title><desc id="s60-d">A jailbreak tricks an unchanged model with a cleverly worded prompt, and the company can patch it. An uncensored model is a downloaded copy that someone has altered, by retraining or abliteration, so the change is built into the file and nobody can patch it centrally. Illegal content is illegal from either.</desc><defs><marker id="s60-ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M1 1L9 5L1 9z" fill="#231F20"/></marker></defs><g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="20" y="40" width="190" height="190" fill="#FFE2D5" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115" y="64" font-size="11" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#A7350B">JAILBREAK</text><text x="38" y="96" font-size="11" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20">· model unchanged</text><text x="38" y="122" font-size="11" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20">· a tricky prompt fools it</text><text x="38" y="148" font-size="11" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20">· company can patch it</text><rect x="230" y="40" width="190" height="190" fill="#FCEBEB" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="325" y="64" font-size="11" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9b1c14">UNCENSORED MODEL</text><text x="248" y="96" font-size="11" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20">· the file itself altered</text><text x="248" y="122" font-size="11" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20">· by retraining or abliteration</text><text x="248" y="148" font-size="11" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20">· runs on someone's own</text><text x="248" y="174" font-size="11" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20">· computer: no patch</text><rect x="20" y="242" width="400" height="38" fill="#FFF3C4" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="220" y="266" font-size="12" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">Either way, illegal content is still illegal.</text></g></svg>

s61.title: Learn from answers, then test on new ones
s61.caption: Supervised learning trains on examples that come with the right answers. The honest test is on examples kept back from training: a model can score well on what it has seen and badly on what it hasn't. Made-up numbers.

s68.title: Each model learns what is left over
s68.caption: Gradient boosting adds small models one at a time, each trained on the errors still left. It is one of the most accurate methods for tables of data. Made-up numbers.

Adding its corrections shrinks the error; the next model learns what is left over again. s69.title: Three ways to make better features
s69.caption: Models only see numbers, and they learn faster from numbers that capture what matters. Combining, transforming and encoding raw data are three common ways to make better features. Made-up example.

Combine: 36 books in 3 years becomes 12 books a year. Transform: a date of birth becomes an age. s70.title: The sweet spot between too simple and too complex
s70.caption: Overfitting shows up as a gap: training error keeps falling while error on new data starts rising. Checking on kept-back data shows where to stop.
s70.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s70-t s70-d"><title id="s70-t">The sweet spot between too simple and too complex</title><desc id="s70-d">As a model gets more complex, its error on training data keeps falling. Its error on new data falls at first, then rises once it starts memorising noise: that is overfitting. The best model sits at the lowest point of the new-data curve. More data, simpler models and stopping early all help.</desc><defs><marker id="s70-ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M1 1L9 5L1 9z" fill="#231F20"/></marker></defs><g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif"><path d="M40 30 V220 H410" fill="none" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="36" y="26" font-size="9.5" font-weight="400" text-anchor="start" fill="#5f5a52">error ↑</text><text x="220" y="236" font-size="10.5" font-weight="400" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f5a52">model complexity →</text><path d="M50 66 C120 160 200 195 400 208" fill="none" stroke="#006A7D" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M50 56 C120 135 170 158 210 156 S320 110 400 60" fill="none" stroke="#9b1c14" stroke-width="3"/><text x="392" y="196" font-size="11" font-weight="800" text-anchor="end" fill="#006A7D">training data</text><text x="392" y="54" font-size="11" font-weight="800" text-anchor="end" fill="#9b1c14">new data</text><line x1="205" y1="52" x2="205" y2="220" stroke="#176E3B" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="205" y="44" font-size="11" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#176E3B">sweet spot</text><text x="100" y="214" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f5a52">too simple</text><text x="330" y="140" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9b1c14">overfitting:</text><text x="330" y="154" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9b1c14">memorising noise</text><rect x="20" y="248" width="400" height="34" fill="#DDF8E7" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="220" y="270" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">Helps: more data · a simpler model · stopping training early</text></g></svg>

s71.title: Learn what is normal, flag what is far from it
s71.caption: Anomaly detection learns a picture of normal and scores how far each new event is from it. Flags are for a person to check: unusual isn't always wrong. Made-up example.
s71.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s71-t s71-d"><title id="s71-t">Learn what is normal, flag what is far from it</title><desc id="s71-d">Anomaly detection first learns what normal looks like, such as usual payment amounts, times and places. Each new event gets a score for how far it is from normal. Events past a threshold are flagged for a person to check, because some unusual events are innocent.</desc><defs><marker id="s71-ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M1 1L9 5L1 9z" fill="#231F20"/></marker></defs><g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif"><text x="20" y="24" font-size="13" font-weight="800" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20" letter-spacing=".08em">CARD PAYMENTS: HOW UNUSUAL?</text><path d="M40 40 V200 H410" fill="none" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="410" y="214" font-size="9.5" font-weight="400" text-anchor="end" fill="#5f5a52">how unusual →</text><path d="M50 190 C90 190 100 70 140 70 S190 190 230 192" fill="#D6F4FA" stroke="#006A7D" stroke-width="2"/><text x="140" y="62" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#006A7D">normal: £2–£10, daytime, UK</text><line x1="280" y1="50" x2="280" y2="200" stroke="#A7350B" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="284" y="60" font-size="10.5" font-weight="800" text-anchor="start" fill="#A7350B">threshold</text><circle cx="390" cy="180" r="7" fill="#F7C1C1" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.2"/><circle cx="320" cy="180" r="7" fill="#F7C1C1" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="294" y="100" font-size="10" font-weight="700" text-anchor="start" fill="#9b1c14">£950, 3am, abroad</text><text x="294" y="138" font-size="10" font-weight="700" text-anchor="start" fill="#5f5a52">£40 trip</text><line x1="380" y1="104" x2="390" y2="172" stroke="#9b1c14" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="312" y1="142" x2="320" y2="172" stroke="#5f5a52" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="20" y="226" width="400" height="54" fill="#FFF3C4" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="220" y="248" font-size="11" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">Flagged for a person to check: the £40 school trip</text><text x="220" y="264" font-size="11" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">was unusual but fine. s72.title: A forecast is a range, not a point
s72.caption: Good forecasts come with a range. The further ahead they look, the wider it gets: next week is easier to predict than next term. Made-up numbers.
s72.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 280" role="img" aria-labelledby="s72-t s72-d"><title id="s72-t">A forecast is a range, not a point</title><desc id="s72-d">Past weekly lunch numbers are drawn as a line. The forecast continues the line, with a shaded band showing the likely range, which gets wider the further ahead it looks, because uncertainty grows.</desc><defs><marker id="s72-ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M1 1L9 5L1 9z" fill="#231F20"/></marker></defs><g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif"><text x="20" y="24" font-size="13" font-weight="800" text-anchor="start" fill="#231F20" letter-spacing=".08em">LUNCHES SOLD EACH WEEK</text><path d="M40 40 V220 H410" fill="none" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="410" y="234" font-size="9.5" font-weight="400" text-anchor="end" fill="#5f5a52">weeks →</text><polyline points="50,150 80,140 110,156 140,132 170,144 200,126 230,138" fill="none" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="230,138 400,72 400,168" fill="#FDE3F9" stroke="none"/><line x1="230" y1="138" x2="400" y2="120" stroke="#983488" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><line x1="230" y1="48" x2="230" y2="220" stroke="#5f5a52" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><text x="226" y="58" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="end" fill="#5f5a52">past</text><text x="236" y="58" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="start" fill="#983488">forecast</text><text x="396" y="66" font-size="10.5" font-weight="800" text-anchor="end" fill="#983488">wider further ahead</text><text x="220" y="252" font-size="12" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#983488">Plan for the range, not just the middle line.</text></g></svg>

s73.title: Trend, season and the rest
s73.caption: Time-series methods often split data into a trend, a repeating season and leftover noise. A jump that is just "summer again" isn't news; a change in the trend might be. Made-up data.

s74.title: From what happened to what will happen
s74.caption: Predictive analytics turns past data into a likely future, stated with how sure it is. It is the third of four common analytics steps, before deciding what to do. Made-up numbers.

s79.title: From words to an action
s79.caption: Language processing turns messy human words into something a computer can act on: what you want (the intent) and the details. Today's large language models handle several of these steps in one go.

s80.title: What a computer sees in a picture
s80.caption: Computer vision starts from numbers, one per pixel, and builds up from edges to shapes to objects. Like any model, it can be fooled by things it rarely saw in training, such as unusual lighting.

s81.title: How an AI answer chooses its sources
s81.caption: Generative engine optimisation tries to get pages cited in AI answers. One study (Aggarwal and others, 2024) found adding citations, quotations and statistics helped most, but results vary and added numbers still need to be true.

s82.title: Analysing versus creating
s82.caption: Generative AI learns patterns from huge numbers of examples, then produces new text, images, audio, video or code that fit them. The output is what is likely, not what is checked.
s82.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s82-t s82-d"><title id="s82-t">Analysing versus creating</title><desc id="s82-d">Given the same kind of data, analytical AI answers a question about it, such as "is this a cat?", while generative AI makes something new that fits the patterns it learned: a new cat picture, a poem, a voice or code. s85.title: A forger and a detective
s85.caption: A GAN trains a generator and a discriminator against each other. When the discriminator can only guess, right about half the time, the fakes are realistic. Diffusion models have since overtaken GANs for most image tools. Made-up numbers.
s85.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s85-t s85-d"><title id="s85-t">A forger and a detective</title><desc id="s85-d">A generative adversarial network has two parts. The generator makes fake pictures; the discriminator sees real and fake ones and guesses which is which. Each learns from the other: the generator from being caught, the discriminator from its mistakes. Training aims for fakes the discriminator can only guess at, right about half the time.</desc><defs><marker id="s85-ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M1 1L9 5L1 9z" fill="#231F20"/></marker></defs><g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="20" y="50" width="120" height="70" fill="#ECE5FF" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="80" y="72" font-size="10.5" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6441B8">GENERATOR</text><text x="80" y="92" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">the forger:</text><text x="80" y="106" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">makes fakes</text><rect x="20" y="140" width="120" height="50" fill="#D6F4FA" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="80" y="160" font-size="11" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">real photos</text><text x="80" y="178" font-size="9.5" font-weight="400" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f5a52">from the training set</text><line x1="142" y1="85" x2="196" y2="112" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#s85-ar)"/><line x1="142" y1="165" x2="196" y2="132" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#s85-ar)"/><rect x="198" y="90" width="120" height="70" fill="#FFE2D5" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="258" y="112" font-size="10.5" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#A7350B">DISCRIMINATOR</text><text x="258" y="132" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">the detective:</text><text x="258" y="146" font-size="10.5" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">real or fake?</text><path d="M258 88 Q195.0 92.4 142 58" fill="none" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="4 4" marker-end="url(#s85-ar)"/><text x="232" y="50" font-size="10" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f5a52">caught! s90.title: Thinking before answering
s90.caption: Reasoning models are trained to work through a problem, and check their steps, before answering. They do better at maths, coding and logic, but are slower and cost more, and their steps can still go wrong.

The extra thinking helps with maths, code and logic, but takes longer and costs more.</desc><defs><marker id="s90-ar" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M1 1L9 5L1 9z" fill="#231F20"/></marker></defs><g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif"><rect x="20" y="36" width="400" height="40" fill="#FFF3C4" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="220" y="52" font-size="11" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#231F20">A bat and a ball cost £1.10. s91.title: Useful extra data, with a catch
s91.caption: Synthetic data fills gaps and protects privacy. A 2024 Nature study (Shumailov and others) showed that models trained over and over on generated data lose the rare cases first, so real data must stay in the mix.

s92.title: Stop, check the source, report
s92.caption: Deepfakes are getting too good to spot by eye, so check the source, not just the pixels. In England and Wales, creating a sexual deepfake of an adult without consent has been a crime since 6 February 2026; any sexual image of an under-18 is illegal. Young people can use Childline's Report Remove.

s94.caption: Context engineering decides what the model gets to read: rules, documents, examples, tool results, memory and the question. The window has a limit, so choosing what to leave out matters as much as what to put in.

s96.title: Cheap to make, costly to sort through
s96.caption: AI slop spreads because it costs almost nothing to make and clicks still pay. It drowns out real work and can mislead. Check for a named source, and don't feed it with shares.

s101.title: Many tools, one process
s101.caption: Hyperautomation, a term Gartner popularised in 2019, means combining many automation and AI tools across whole processes. Not every step should be automated: people keep the judgement calls.

s102.title: What starts an automation
s102.caption: Trigger, condition, action: the shape of almost every automation. A badly chosen trigger can fire too often, or never, so test it.

s103.title: Act the moment it happens
s103.caption: Event-driven automations react as things happen instead of checking on a timer. That is faster and wastes fewer checks, but the system sending the events has to be reliable.

s104.title: A message sent the moment something happens
s104.caption: A webhook is one app calling another's web address the moment something happens, with the details attached. Because anyone could send to that address, the receiver should check a signature.

s113.title: It suggests; you decide
s113.caption: Copilots speed up drafting by suggesting as you work. In one controlled study (Peng and others, 2023) developers finished a coding task 55.8% faster. Checking what you accept is still your job.
